body:
Problem: No way to configure the lockfile location.

Solution: Add 'packlockfile' option.

---

I have no strong opinions on the option name or value. The choice was made to be as similar as possible to a somewhat similar `'shadafile'` option: ~~`''` does nothing, non-empty value overrides the default lockfile path.~~

The `'packlockpath'` name feels too close to something like `'packpath'`, `'runtimepath'`, etc. which are lists of paths (not a single path).

---

Resolves #36078. Like by setting `vim.o.packlockfile = vim.fs.joinpath(vim.fn.stdpath('data'), 'nvim-pack-lock.json')` before the first call of any `vim.pack` function.

There is still an open door to disabling lockfile related functionality completely (probably by `set packlockfile=NONE`, as in `'shadafile'`). But looking at code several times, I do think that it will add too much complexity for a (what feels like) not big of a gain.

comment_data.body:
`lock_get_path()` is [duplicated in `pack/health.lua` as `get_lockfile_path()`](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/40562/changes#diff-e69a6d2511175aaa81d0b172d871b2f5b0309314bce63e37fe0ef23828881d1fR5-R10). The easy fix would simply be to import this function inside of `pack/health.lua`, but I have a possible other idea:

What if instead of `'packlockfile'` defaulting to an empty string, it instead defaults to `"$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nvim/nvim-pack-lock.json"`? That way, `lock_get_path()` could just be removed altogether and replaced with just `vim.go.packlockfile`.

This would also make it easier for plugins/configs to refer to the location of the lockfile, since they can also just use `vim.go.packlockfile` directly instead of having to reinvent their own version of `lock_get_path()`.

comment_data.body:
> `lock_get_path()` is [duplicated in `pack/health.lua` as `get_lockfile_path()`](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/40562/changes#diff-e69a6d2511175aaa81d0b172d871b2f5b0309314bce63e37fe0ef23828881d1fR5-R10). The easy fix would simply be to import this function inside of `pack/health.lua`, but I have a possible other idea:

I don't think having to define a two-line function twice is enough of an inconvenience to have to find a way to work around it.

> What if instead of `'packlockfile'` defaulting to an empty string, it instead defaults to `"$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nvim/nvim-pack-lock.json"`? That way, `lock_get_path()` could just be removed altogether and replaced with just `vim.go.packlockfile`.
> 
> This would also make it easier for plugins/configs to refer to the location of the lockfile, since they can also just use `vim.go.packlockfile` directly instead of having to reinvent their own version of `lock_get_path()`.

That was the initial idea indeed and I would go this way in case of `vim.pack.config()`. But I do think that aligning with already present options should be the guide here. And with that, the empty default option value that can override some hard-coded default seems to be the most common approach: 'shadafile', 'spellfile', 'verbosefile'.

There are 'helpfile' and 'errorfile' with default value as path, but they feel less aligned with "permanent store of something". There are as well boolean 'swapfile' and 'undofile'.

Options that end with `path` ('cdpath', 'packpath', 'path', 'runtimepath') all use explicit paths as default, but they are lists of directory paths, not a single file path.

I am open to changing this to default to an explicit `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nvim/nvim-pack-lock.json` (although not sure how and where to set it in code), but the current implementation is what I currently think is best. Would need @justinmk decision on this.

comment_data.body:
> I agree that actual path as a default value is better, 

this :)

> yet I do value consistency with other similar options more.

I am extremely in favor of consistency, but we aren't gaining anything by trying to interpret Vim's "convention" in this case. The legacy option default values are the way they are because of historical mistakes, not because of any useful intention. So continuing that tradition doesn't help anything.

It's useful for option *names* and *structure* to have some sort of predictability, but there is no scenario where any code in the wild ever can make assumptions about default values, so we aren't losing anything by changing that approach (for a new option; never mind that we have chosen to "break" existing option defaults such as 'statusline').

p.s. `nvim_get_option_info2()` gives the option default so "empty" is not a necessary signal that "user didn't change the option".

comment_data.body:
> I agree that actual path as a default value is better,

Oh, one extra side effect that I *think* will happen is that the default option value will be computed before any user's startup code. With `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nvim/nvim-pack-lock.json` as the default it would mean that setting `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` inside 'init.lua' will not point to the expected place (since that variable was already expanded). While on `master` and with the current PR version it will use the latest available environment variable value.

This might matter, for example, when creating reproducible examples that set `$XDG_{CONFIG,STATE}_HOME` values. Not the biggest issue (and using `$NVIM_APPNAME` is probably better), but still.

comment_regular_data.body: `vim.pack` should fail early with an error if `'packlockfile'` is a relative path. Right now it will happily create a lockfile in a relative directory (e.g. `vim.o.packlockfile = './lock'`).

> `vim.pack` should fail early with an error if `'packlockfile'` is a relative path. Right now it will happily create a lockfile in a relative directory (e.g. `vim.o.packlockfile = './lock'`).

I agree that setting a relative lockfile path is doubtfully a good idea, but it should absolutely not be a `vim.pack` responsibility to check this. As 1) I don't think there is a precedent to strongly allow only an absolutae path as a config value; and 2) maybe there *is* a use case for a relative lockfile.

I'd personally prefer to disallow relative lockfiles until a use case is actually presented (which I imagine will simply never happen). I'd imagine it'd just be a source of bugs that a one line `assert()` could fix.

In the end, I admit it doesn't matter that much tho.
